# 1.6 Example 5

## Step 1 – Recognizing an Argument

Take a look at the following passage and ask yourself, **"What is this
passage doing? Is it trying to convince us that something is true?"**

> "Commercials are a boon for students everywhere, since studies have
> shown that each commercial watched safely and permanently increases
> the viewer's I.Q. by an average of 5 points. Imagine that!"

I'd say that this passage contains an argument because it's trying to
prove that one claim is true by citing other claims as evidence. There's
an inference indicator in this passage that might help us to see this,
too. Did you spot it? It's "since."

> "Commercials are a boon for students everywhere, **since** studies
> have shown that each commercial watched safely and permanently
> increases the viewer's I.Q. by an average of 5 points. Imagine that!"

## Step 2 – Analyzing the Argument

As usual, we'll begin our analysis of the argument by asking, **"What is
the ultimate conclusion, or the main claim that this argument is trying
to get us to believe?"**

The inference indicator expression "since" can help us once we decide if
it's a conclusion indicator or a reason indicator. So which is it? Does
"since" introduce a conclusion (making it a conclusion indicator
expression like "therefore") or does it introduce a reason to believe
something else (making it a reason indicator expression like "because")?

Let's figure it out by first replacing the "since" with "therefore,"
then replacing the "since" with "because," and seeing which passage
sounds more like the original.

Here's the original:

> "Commercials are a boon for students everywhere, **since** studies
> have shown that each commercial watched safely and permanently
> increases the viewer's I.Q. by an average of 5 points. Imagine that!"

Here's what we get when we replace "since" with "therefore":

> "Commercials are a boon for students everywhere, **therefore** studies
> have shown that each commercial watched safely and permanently
> increases the viewer's I.Q. by an average of 5 points. Imagine that!"

And here's what we get when we replace "since" with "because":

> "Commercials are a boon for students everywhere, **because** studies
> have shown that each commercial watched safely and permanently
> increases the viewer's I.Q. by an average of 5 points. Imagine that!"

It seems to me that the second passage is more like the original, which
means that "since" is more like "because." It's a reason indicator
expression. This tells us that "studies have shown that each commercial
watched safely and permanently increases the viewer's I.Q. by an average
of 5 points" is being given as a reason to believe "Commercials are a
boon for students everywhere." And this, in turn, means that
"Commercials are a boon for students everywhere" is the conclusion.

> "(1) Commercials are a boon for students everywhere, **since** studies
> have shown that each commercial watched safely and permanently
> increases the viewer's I.Q. by an average of 5 points. Imagine that!"

Our next questions are, **"What else is being claimed?"** and **"Is this
claim part of the argument?"**

The claim "studies have shown that each commercial watched safely and
permanently increases the viewer's I.Q. by an average of 5 points" is
definitely important. We know this because it's introduced with the word
"since." Because "since" is a reason indicator expression, this shows
that the claim that follows it is being given as a reason in support of
something else.

> "(1) Commercials are a boon for students everywhere, **since** (2)
> studies have shown that each commercial watched safely and permanently
> increases the viewer's I.Q. by an average of 5 points. Imagine that!"

But what about the last sentence, "Imagine that!"? Should this go in our
list?

As we've seen, claims are either true or false, so a test for
determining whether or not a sentence expresses a claim is to see
whether or not it makes any sense for us to agree or disagree with it.
We've also seen that questions (like "What is the evidence for that?")
can't be true or false and so don't convey claims.

Sentences that tell us to do something, like "Buy this product," and
"Please change the channel" can't be true or false either, since it
wouldn't make much sense for you to say "False!" if I said, "Buy this
product" or "Please change the channel." (Of course, you could refuse to
*obey* me, but that's not the same as saying that my order or request
is false.) We'll call these kinds of sentences "commands." **Commands
usually don't convey claims because they usually can't be true or
false** and so they won't be included in the argument. Let's just ignore
the last sentence of this passage.

(Will we always be ignoring commands? No. As with questions, in a
subsequent chapter we'll see special kinds of commands that do in fact
convey claims, but for now we'll be ignoring commands because *normal*
commands can't be true or false and because in this chapter we'll only
be dealing with normal commands.)

Now that we have some claims identified, we can ask, **"How are these
claims connected to each other?"** And as often happens, there's an
inference indicator expression to help us out. (Whenever you see
inference indicator expressions, take full advantage of them! They live
to serve.) The "since" tells us that claim 2 is being given as a reason
to believe claim 1, so we'll map the argument like this:

> "(1) Commercials are a boon for students everywhere, **since** (2)
> studies have shown that each commercial watched safely and permanently
> increases the viewer's I.Q. by an average of 5 points. Imagine that!"

![Map of the commercials argument.](/images/ch01/Advertisement5.png){#fig-1-6-ad-1 width=289px fig-alt="Argument map concluding: 1) Commercials are a boon for students everywhere. A full text description is provided."}

::: {.map-outline fig="fig-1-6-ad-1"}
{{< include /outlines/ch01/Advertisement5_list.md >}}
:::

We're now ready to evaluate this argument.

## Step 3 – Evaluating the Argument

Let's start with the premise, "studies have shown that each commercial
watched safely and permanently increases the viewer's I.Q. by an average
of 5 points," asking, **"Is this premise true?"** and **"Could someone
who doesn't already believe the ultimate conclusion believe this
premise?"**

I'd say that this premise is bad because it's false. (At least I
strongly *suspect* that it's false.) And if a premise is false, we don't
need to worry about whether it assumes the conclusion. That's enough, on
its own, to make the argument bad.

> "(1) Commercials are a boon for students everywhere, **since** (2)
> studies have shown that each commercial watched safely and permanently
> increases the viewer's I.Q. by an average of 5 points. Imagine that!"

![Map of the commercials argument, with the premise evaluated as false.](/images/ch01/Advertisement5_P_Eval.png){#fig-1-6-ad-p-eval-1 width=289px fig-alt="Argument map concluding: 1) Commercials are a boon for students everywhere. A full text description is provided."}

::: {.map-outline fig="fig-1-6-ad-p-eval-1"}
{{< include /outlines/ch01/Advertisement5_P_Eval_list.md >}}
:::

Note: This argument is bad because it has a bad premise.

But even though this argument is bad, let's talk about it some more. In
particular, let's examine the inference, just for practice. What do you
think? Is the connection between the premise and the conclusion strong?

It's very tempting to say that this inference is bad, thinking that
because claim 2 is *false* it can't establish the truth of 1. But this
way of thinking is mistaken since it doesn't really focus on the
*inference*. It focuses on the premise instead, and (as we've seen)
inferences are not premises.

Remember the Gully Test for evaluating inferences? Let's use it now.
We'll ask ourselves, **"If a perfectly gullible, perfectly rational
person (Gully) believes the reasons, how likely is he to believe the
conclusion?"** What do you think?

It seems to me that if Gully believes that each commercial watched
increases the viewer's I.Q. by an average of 5 points (which he would
believe, because he's gullible and accepts all premises), he'd be
strongly inclined to believe that commercials are a boon for students
everywhere (because he's rational, and it's rational to think that
students would benefit from boosting their I.Q.). Of course, Gully
*could* doubt the importance of IQ for academic success, which means
that Gully isn't *compelled* to think that commercials are a boon for
students everywhere, but it's reasonable to suppose that Gully
*probably* would agree with the conclusion once he's told the premise.
This means that the inference is good, even though the premise is bad.
(The Gully Test is designed to help us to appreciate good inferences
even when we, personally, reject the premises.)

> "(1) Commercials are a boon for students everywhere, **since** (2)
> studies have shown that each commercial watched safely and permanently
> increases the viewer's I.Q. by an average of 5 points. Imagine that!"

![Map of the commercials argument, with the premise evaluated as false and the inference evaluated as good.](/images/ch01/Advertisement5_I_Eval.png){#fig-1-6-ad-i-eval-1 width=292px fig-alt="Argument map concluding: 1) Commercials are a boon for students everywhere. A full text description is provided."}

::: {.map-outline fig="fig-1-6-ad-i-eval-1"}
{{< include /outlines/ch01/Advertisement5_I_Eval_list.md >}}
:::

Note: This argument is bad because it has a bad premise.

The Gully Method is a great way to evaluate inferences because it can be
applied to any argument. It also demonstrates why it's nice to be able
to evaluate an inference even when we disagree with the premise.
Evaluating inferences helps us to see how rationally the author of the
argument is thinking, and it's very useful to realize when the author is
thinking rationally, *especially if* the author has beliefs, expressed
as premises, that we don't share—as is the case here.

This argument is still *bad*, of course, because the premise is still
bad. An argument is good only if it establishes the truth of its
ultimate conclusion. Since the premise is false, it can't establish that
the ultimate conclusion is true. The good inference isn't enough to save
this argument but it's nice to see that the inference *is* good because
it enables us to see that even though we disagree with the author's
premise, we agree with the author's 'logic,' so to speak.

### Communicating Our Evaluation

We've already seen that we shouldn't criticize the person offering the
argument or make their mistakes seem outrageous. It's even *better* if
we can **find something in the argument with which we *agree***. This
shows that we respect the author of the argument, and *that* helps to
build the trust necessary to talk about controversial subjects and solve
difficult problems.

This argument, for instance, has a false premise but a reasonably good
inference.

> "(1) Commercials are a boon for students everywhere, **since** (2)
> studies have shown that each commercial watched safely and permanently
> increases the viewer's I.Q. by an average of 5 points. Imagine that!"

![Map of the commercials argument, with the premise evaluated as false and the inference evaluated as good.](/images/ch01/Advertisement5_I_Eval.png){#fig-1-6-ad-i-eval-2 width=292px fig-alt="Argument map concluding: 1) Commercials are a boon for students everywhere. A full text description is provided."}

::: {.map-outline fig="fig-1-6-ad-i-eval-2"}
{{< include /outlines/ch01/Advertisement5_I_Eval_list.md >}}
:::

Because we think the premise is false, we can say something like, "This
argument assumes that studies have shown that commercials raise a
viewer's I.Q. and that seems unlikely to me. At the very least, I'd want
to review the studies myself."

Because we like the inference, we can conclude our evaluation by saying
something like, "Even though I don't accept that commercials raise
I.Q.s, I certainly do see how the conclusion would follow from that
assumption. I agree that if watching commercials did raise I.Q.'s,
commercials would be a wonderful thing for students!"

### Valid, Good, and Bad Inferences

Evaluating inferences can be a little tricky, so let's think about it
some more.

#### Valid Inferences

To better understand how the strength of the inference between two
claims is independent of the actual truth of either claim, let's
consider the inference from the premise, "Lee is a green-blooded
Martian," to the conclusion, "Lee is a Martian."

![Map of the inference from "Lee is a green-blooded Martian" to "Lee is a Martian."](/images/ch01/Lee1.png){#fig-1-6-lee1 width=260px fig-alt="Argument map concluding: Lee is a Martian. A full text description is provided."}

::: {.map-outline fig="fig-1-6-lee1"}
{{< include /outlines/ch01/Lee1_list.md >}}
:::

I very much doubt that the claims in this argument are true, but we're
not considering the truth of the claims. We're focusing on the
*connection* or *inference* between these two claims, and *that* seems
to be excellent because if "Lee is a green-blooded Martian" *were* true
then "Lee is a Martian" would have to be true as well.

We can see this with the Gully Test. We tell Gully, "You know, Lee is a
green-blooded Martian." Gully, being gullible, would probably say, "Wow.
That's interesting!" How likely would Gully be to believe that Lee is a
Martian at that point? Gully simply couldn't *avoid* thinking that Lee
is a Martian! To think that Lee is a green-blooded Martian without
thinking that Lee is a Martian would be irrational. And Gully is
rational. The conclusion is forced upon Gully, once Gully accepts the
premise.

We call perfect inferences like this "valid inferences." **When we say
that an inference is valid, we mean that if the premise were true (which
it might not actually be) then the conclusion would *have* to be true as
well (which, again, it might not actually be)**.

![Map of the inference from "Lee is a green-blooded Martian" to "Lee is a Martian," evaluated as valid.](/images/ch01/Lee1_I_Eval.png){#fig-1-6-lee1-eval width=289px fig-alt="Argument map concluding: Lee is a Martian. A full text description is provided."}

::: {.map-outline fig="fig-1-6-lee1-eval"}
{{< include /outlines/ch01/Lee1_I_Eval_list.md >}}
:::

(By the way, whenever we use the word "valid" we'll be referring to
inferences. Outside logic and critical thinking, we can talk about a
point or claim being valid. But not here. Here only *inferences* are
valid. For us, points and claims aren't valid; they're good or bad, true
or false, but they aren't valid or invalid.)

#### Good Inferences

Of course, not every inference is valid. In fact, very few inferences
are valid. "Valid," after all, means "perfect" and almost *everything*
falls short of perfection. Almost all inferences are imperfect, or
*invalid*.

When we say that the inference between a reason and a conclusion is
*good* (although not perfect), we mean that if the reason were true then
the conclusion would *most likely* be true as well, although it
wouldn't *have* to be true.

For example, consider the inference from the premise, "Lee is a
green-blooded Martian," to the conclusion, "Lee believes in
extra-terrestrial life."

![Map of the inference from "Lee is a green-blooded Martian" to "Lee believes in extra-terrestrial life."](/images/ch01/Lee2.png){#fig-1-6-lee2 width=274px fig-alt="Argument map concluding: Lee believes in extra-terrestrial life. A full text description is provided."}

::: {.map-outline fig="fig-1-6-lee2"}
{{< include /outlines/ch01/Lee2_list.md >}}
:::

It doesn't matter whether or not either of these claims is actually
true. The question is "If it *were* true that Lee is a green-blooded
Martian, *would* it be true that Lee believes in extra-terrestrial
life?"

I think that the answer to this question is "Very likely, but not for
certain." After all, maybe Lee is suffering from amnesia. Maybe Lee
doesn\'t *know* that Lee is a green-blooded Martian. Nonetheless,
barring such a situation, I think that Lee probably would believe in
extra-terrestrial life if Lee were a green-blooded Martian, and so I'd
say that this inference is good even though it isn't perfect.

The Gully Test would get us the same result, of course. If we tell
Gully, "Lee is a green-blooded Martian," Gully would think that Lee
*probably* believes in extra-terrestrial life, but Gully would recognize
that Lee might not believe in extra-terrestrial life for the reason that
we just discussed. Once again, the inference turns out to be good but
not perfect.

![Map of the inference from "Lee is a green-blooded Martian" to "Lee believes in extra-terrestrial life," evaluated as good but not perfect.](/images/ch01/Lee2_I_Eval.png){#fig-1-6-lee2-eval width=379px fig-alt="Argument map concluding: Lee believes in extra-terrestrial life. A full text description is provided."}

::: {.map-outline fig="fig-1-6-lee2-eval"}
{{< include /outlines/ch01/Lee2_I_Eval_list.md >}}
:::

#### Bad Inferences

When we say that the inference between a reason and a conclusion is
*bad*, we mean that if the reason were true, the conclusion could *very
easily* still be false. The reason has very little bearing upon the
conclusion.

For example, consider the inference from the premise, "Lee is a
green-blooded Martian," to the conclusion, "Lee likes pepperoni pizza."

![Map of the inference from "Lee is a green-blooded Martian" to "Lee likes pepperoni pizza."](/images/ch01/Lee3.png){#fig-1-6-lee3 width=260px fig-alt="Argument map concluding: Lee likes pepperoni pizza. A full text description is provided."}

::: {.map-outline fig="fig-1-6-lee3"}
{{< include /outlines/ch01/Lee3_list.md >}}
:::

This inference is bad because even if Lee *were* a green-blooded
Martian, Lee could still *very easily* not like pepperoni pizza. If we
told Gully, "Lee is a green-blooded Martian," Gully would not be likely
to accept that Lee likes pepperoni pizza on that basis. Any way you look
at it, this inference is horrible.

![Map of the inference from "Lee is a green-blooded Martian" to "Lee likes pepperoni pizza," evaluated as bad.](/images/ch01/Lee3_I_Eval.png){#fig-1-6-lee3-eval width=284px fig-alt="Argument map concluding: Lee likes pepperoni pizza. A full text description is provided."}

::: {.map-outline fig="fig-1-6-lee3-eval"}
{{< include /outlines/ch01/Lee3_I_Eval_list.md >}}
:::

#### Degrees of Goodness

Note that although "valid" and "invalid" (as well as "strong" and
"weak") are reserved for inferences, and although "true" and "false" are
reserved for claims, both claims *and* inferences can be described as
"good" and "bad." Most of the time we'll use "good" and "bad" for
exactly this reason. We won't have to worry about whether or not we're
using the right kind of term because "good" and "bad" cover everything.

As we've seen, inferences come in *degrees* of goodness, lying on a
continuum from very bad to perfect, or valid. (Validity *itself*, of
course, doesn't come in degrees. An inference can't be "sort of" valid
just like something can't be "sort of" perfect. Either something is
perfect, or it isn't. Either an inference is valid, or it's not.)

Once we start talking about degrees of goodness, it can be difficult to
decide how good something needs to be. How good an inference needs to be
in order to be "good enough" is largely a matter of context and personal
preference. Under some circumstances (say when deciding if a plane is
safe to fly) we want our inferences to be *very* good because the stakes
are high. Under other circumstances (say when deciding whether or not to
attend a certain movie) we can make do with weaker inferences because it
doesn't really matter much if we make a mistake. Similarly, some people
are just more risk-averse than others, and they'll hold inferences to a
fairly high standard most of the time. Other people are more comfortable
with error, and they'll accept less certainty in their reasoning.

## Summary of Example 5

Here's the passage that we considered in this example:

> "Commercials are a boon for students everywhere, since studies have
> shown that each commercial watched safely and permanently increases
> the viewer's I.Q. by an average of 5 points. Imagine that!"

### Step 1 – Recognizing an Argument

We asked, **"What is this passage doing? Is it trying to convince us
that something is true?"**

We decided that this passage is trying to convince us of something and
so does contain an argument. The inference indicator expression "since"
helped us, too.

> "Commercials are a boon for students everywhere, **since** studies
> have shown that each commercial watched safely and permanently
> increases the viewer's I.Q. by an average of 5 points. Imagine that!"

### Step 2 – Analyzing the Argument

Our first question when analyzing this argument was, **"What is the
ultimate conclusion, or the main claim that this argument is trying to
get us to believe?"**

The fact that "since" is a reason indicator expression allowed us to see
that "studies have shown that each commercial watched safely and
permanently increases the viewer's I.Q. by an average of 5 points" is
being given as a reason to believe "commercials are a boon for students
everywhere," making "commercials are a boon for students everywhere" the
ultimate conclusion of this argument.

> "(1) Commercials are a boon for students everywhere, **since** studies
> have shown that each commercial watched safely and permanently
> increases the viewer's I.Q. by an average of 5 points. Imagine that!"

Our next questions were, **"What else is being claimed?"** and **"Is
this claim part of the argument?"**

Because "since" is an inference indicator, we knew that the claim that
follows it is part of the argument.

> "(1) Commercials are a boon for students everywhere, **since** (2)
> studies have shown that each commercial watched safely and permanently
> increases the viewer's I.Q. by an average of 5 points. Imagine that!"

"Imagine that," on the other hand, is a command sentence. Commands
usually don't contain claims because they usually can't be true or
false. We ignored that sentence.

At this point, we asked, **"How are these claims connected to each
other?"** "Since" has already allowed us to see that claim 2 is a reason
to accept claim 1, so we mapped the argument like this:

> "(1) Commercials are a boon for students everywhere, **since** (2)
> studies have shown that each commercial watched safely and permanently
> increases the viewer's I.Q. by an average of 5 points. Imagine that!"

![Map of the commercials argument.](/images/ch01/Advertisement5.png){#fig-1-6-ad-2 width=289px fig-alt="Argument map concluding: 1) Commercials are a boon for students everywhere. A full text description is provided."}

::: {.map-outline fig="fig-1-6-ad-2"}
{{< include /outlines/ch01/Advertisement5_list.md >}}
:::

### Step 3 – Evaluating the Argument

We evaluated the premise by asking **"Is this premise true?"** and
**"Could someone who doesn't already believe the ultimate conclusion
believe this premise?"**

We decided that this premise is bad because it's false. That's enough to
make the argument bad as a whole.

> "(1) Commercials are a boon for students everywhere, **since** (2)
> studies have shown that each commercial watched safely and permanently
> increases the viewer's I.Q. by an average of 5 points. Imagine that!"

![Map of the commercials argument, with the premise evaluated as false.](/images/ch01/Advertisement5_P_Eval.png){#fig-1-6-ad-p-eval-2 width=289px fig-alt="Argument map concluding: 1) Commercials are a boon for students everywhere. A full text description is provided."}

::: {.map-outline fig="fig-1-6-ad-p-eval-2"}
{{< include /outlines/ch01/Advertisement5_P_Eval_list.md >}}
:::

Note: This argument is bad because it has a bad premise.

![](/images/ch01/sad_face.png){.illustration width=40px fig-alt="A sad face."}

Just for practice, we evaluated the inference by asking, **"If a
perfectly gullible, perfectly rational person (Gully) believes the
reasons, how likely is he to believe the conclusion?"**

We decided that the inference was pretty good!

> "(1) Commercials are a boon for students everywhere, **since** (2)
> studies have shown that each commercial watched safely and permanently
> increases the viewer's I.Q. by an average of 5 points. Imagine that!"

![Map of the commercials argument, with the premise evaluated as false and the inference evaluated as good.](/images/ch01/Advertisement5_I_Eval.png){#fig-1-6-ad-i-eval-3 width=292px fig-alt="Argument map concluding: 1) Commercials are a boon for students everywhere. A full text description is provided."}

::: {.map-outline fig="fig-1-6-ad-i-eval-3"}
{{< include /outlines/ch01/Advertisement5_I_Eval_list.md >}}
:::

Note: This argument is bad because it has a bad premise.

This doesn't make the argument good, of course, but it does give us
something *good to say* about the argument when we express our
evaluation. "Even though I doubt studies have shown that commercials
raise a viewer's I.Q.," we can say, "I agree that if watching
commercials raised I.Q.'s, it would be a wonderful thing for students!"

It's a good idea to find something good to say about an argument, even
when the argument is bad. It keeps the lines of communication open.
